headlineLines: The system tells them weeks later.
standfirst: A concept for the person nobody designs for: the site study coordinator, whose whole job is keeping patients inside a date range that lives in a spreadsheet.

items.value: Problem framing · Product design · Design system

cards.label: THE PROBLEM
cards.body: Every trial patient must be seen inside a date range calculated from their own randomisation date. Sponsor systems record that a visit happened; they do not compute when the next one must. So coordinators keep that maths in a spreadsheet — and a spreadsheet cannot warn anyone.

cards.label: WHAT WE DID
cards.body: Rebuilt the day around the window rather than the record. A worklist instead of a dashboard, every date shown as a window with time remaining, and a justification captured at the moment a rule has to be broken.

cards.label: WHAT IT WOULD CHANGE
cards.body: A missed window stops being something discovered at the next monitoring visit and becomes something visible while it can still be prevented. Not measured — this is a concept, and the section below states what we would test.

headlineLines: And it lives in a spreadsheet.
paragraphs: Every visit in a clinical trial has to happen inside a date range calculated per patient — protocol day, plus or minus the allowed days, counted from that patient's own randomisation date. Miss it and the visit becomes a protocol deviation that has to be explained to the sponsor.

The sponsor's system records that a visit happened. It does not compute when the next one must. So the coordinator keeps that arithmetic in their own spreadsheet, alongside three or four other trials, each with a different sponsor, a different portal and a different login.

panel.label: ONE PATIENT · ONE MISSED WINDOW
panel.footnote: Weeks between the miss and anyone knowing · by then it can only be documented, not prevented

headlineLines: We interviewed nobody. So here is exactly what this is built

items.body: That coordinators, not sponsors, would be given a tool of their own. Commercially this is the hardest assumption, because the sponsor holds the budget.
That window arithmetic can be derived reliably from the protocol without manual configuration for every study.
That a justification captured at booking time is acceptable to sponsors and auditors as the deviation record itself.
That site staff will adopt one more system, when fewer systems is the thing they actually ask for.

blocks.note: This is self-initiated work. There is no client, no user research and no proprietary data, and every number on the screens is illustrative. The problem framing comes from publicly documented pain in clinical research operations plus the four assumptions above. We would rather show you the reasoning and its holes than dress a concept up as a case study with invented results.

blocks.headline: Our first version was a dashboard. We threw it away.
paragraphs: It was a good dashboard: enrollment against plan, site health, open queries, protocol deviations, all in one calm view. It also solved nothing. Every CTMS on the market already ships that screen, and it fails the same way they all do — it reports the problem accurately, after the problem has happened.

The fix was not a better dashboard. It was changing whose day the product is built around. A study manager needs oversight across many sites; a coordinator needs to get through today at one site. Same data, opposite job — and the interface follows whoever signs the contract. That rejected dashboard is still in the file, kept on purpose.

blocks.headline: A worklist, not a dashboard
paragraphs: The home screen answers one question: what must I do today. It opens on two groups only — windows closing now, and windows closing this week — each row carrying the patient, the visit, the window and the single action that resolves it. Everything a dashboard would show is still in the product; none of it is on this screen.

The trade-off: a study manager gets almost nothing out of this screen. We accepted that. A screen built to serve both roles equally serves neither, so navigation and the home screen change by role — which is more to build and more to explain.

blocks.headline: No date is ever shown alone
paragraphs: Every date in the product is rendered as its window: the range, a marker for where today sits inside it, and how much room is left. A date tells you when something is due. A window tells you whether you still have time to do anything about it — which is the only question the coordinator is actually asking.

The trade-off: a window costs roughly three times the horizontal space of a date. The visit table therefore caps at eight visits per view and pages beyond that, and the worklist rows are taller than a conventional table. We spent density to buy judgement.

shots.caption: Visit windows across one site's patients

blocks.headline: Capture the reason at the moment the rule breaks
paragraphs: When a booking has to fall outside the window, the reason is captured right there — category, root cause, and what happened, in the coordinator's own words. The protocol deviation is filed from that, timestamped, with the audit trail attached and the monitor notified. The deviation writes itself, at the one moment when someone still remembers the detail.

The trade-off: this puts a form in front of someone at their most rushed moment. We cut it to three fields and pre-filled two from the booking, but it is still friction — deliberately. The alternative is reconstructing the same facts six weeks later from memory and source documents.

shots.caption: The deviation, filed with its audit trail

blocks.intro: None of these are negotiable in clinical research, and each one removed an option a cleaner design would have taken.

items.label: REGULATORY
items.body: Any change to submitted trial data needs an attributable, timestamped, permanent record. Nothing here can be silently edited — records are amended, never overwritten — and the audit trail is part of the interface rather than hidden behind an admin view.

items.label: LEGACY
items.body: The sponsor's systems own the data and are not being replaced. This concept reads from and writes to them rather than becoming a system of record, which is also why it can never be the only place a coordinator works.

items.label: COMMERCIAL
items.body: The sponsor holds the budget; the coordinator does the work. A tool designed for the site has to be paid for by someone who will never use it. That is the problem this design does not solve, and pretending otherwise would make everything else here less believable.

items.label: ACCESSIBILITY
items.body: Window state is never carried by colour alone — every state also carries text and position. Site staff work long shifts on whatever hardware the hospital provides, often at small sizes on old displays.

blocks.eyebrow: 07 · WHAT WE WOULD TEST — NOTHING HERE IS MEASURED
blocks.headline: A missed window should be visible the day it happens — not at the next monitoring visit.
blocks.body: This section is where a client case study would put results. This is a concept, so instead it states what we would measure and what would have to be true for it to be worth building. Nothing below is a finding.

measures.key: Missed windows per 100 visits, baselined against the site's own previous two quarters
Elapsed time between a window closing and the deviation being filed
Coordinator hours per week spent maintaining the tracking spreadsheet
Deviation records returned by the monitor as incomplete or unclear

blocks.footnote: No figure on this page is a measurement. The three criteria above are the thresholds we would agree with a site before building anything — stated up front so that the concept can fail honestly rather than be defended after the fact.

blocks.quote: Move the moment of discovery earlier. Show the window while it is still open — not the deviation after it has closed.
blocks.attributionNote: Written first · every screen was judged against it

blocks.headline: Built as a concept, in full.

columns.title: Problem framing
columns.body: A written framing document: the user, the job to be done, four named failure moments, why the existing category misses them, the design bet, and the four assumptions this rests on — including the commercial one that would most likely kill it.

columns.title: Product design
columns.body: Eight desktop screens at 1440 following one coordinator through one job — worklist, visit-window matrix, booking conflict, out-of-window justification, filed deviation with audit trail, and query resolution with source context. Wired into a clickable prototype with 21 connections.

columns.title: Design system
columns.body: 82 variables across four collections with light and dark modes, 14 text styles, 3 elevation styles, and a component library behind every screen. Checked programmatically: zero unbound fills or strokes across all eight screens.
